payload.title: What Are the Chinese Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
protect_keywords: weird and wonderful chinese wedding traditions (old URL; SEO to quantify US and AU)
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, often with a Chinese-Australian partner or parents (Cantonese, Hokkien, Teochew or other heritage), who want to understand which customs the family may expect, what each looks like on the day, and whether to marry in China (Smartraveller: exercise a high degree of caution overall) or weave the tea ceremony and banquet into a wedding at home or elsewhere.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed after the 'for Australians' section.
payload.angle: Most lists treat Chinese weddings as one set of curiosities. We walk the classical sequence, from the Three Letters and Six Rites to the return visit, say once that customs differ by region and community (Cantonese, Hokkien, Teochew and others, and diaspora families in Australia, Singapore and Malaysia), and tie a custom to a community only where a museum or encyclopaedia does. Meanings come from the Palace Museum, Hong Kong Museum of History, Chinese Museum Melbourne, Powerhouse, Britannica and UNESCO (only as far as its text goes); the rest is labelled 'often told'. We finish with what Australians need to marry in China, as Smartraveller and the Australian Embassy word it, or to bring these rites home.
must_include: One early framing line: customs vary by region, community and family; we name a community only where a source does
About 12 numbered customs in wedding order (batch A rites, then batch B symbols, dress, banquet, red envelopes)
Tea ceremony explained step by step, with UNESCO tea element quoted only as far as its text links to weddings
Hair-combing and door games described as playful, family-led rites; superstitions lightly as 'often told'

Section for Australians: Smartraveller level and update date (as at November 2026), Gyirong County and Tibet/Xinjiang lines neutrally, visa waiver as at November 2026, dual nationality line, Australian Embassy Beijing and Consulates-General Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu for CNI and notarial, 'Getting married overseas', 'check with the registry and the embassy, including any fees'; Chinese-Australian weddings at home
FAQ of 5 to 7 questions with no amounts
